clue.text: Well, this is a bit rich!

definitions.text: Well, this is a bit rich!

parts.words: Well, this is a bit rich!
parts.note: put the solution after the first word, 'Well', and the phrase means wealthy, so this word with 'well' is a description of someone a bit rich

explanation.surface: An indignant exclamation at someone's cheek or hypocrisy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This is a bit rich!' sounds like outrage, but read literally the clue says 'well' plus this word means rich: well-heeled is an idiom for wealthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined to 'well', the word forms an idiom for wealthy, someone with good shoes on their feet.

clue.text: In which passionate couple, unfaithful, ultimately meet?

definitions.text: In which passionate couple, unfaithful, ultimately meet?

parts.note: hot means passionate or ardent

indicators.note: take the closing letter of each of the two preceding words

explanation.surface: Where would an adulterous pair end up having a rendezvous?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a cheating couple's tryst is often in a rented room.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotel is a classic venue for an illicit rendezvous between lovers.

clue.text: Making flat dark?

explanation.surface: Levelling the ground as darkness falls.
explanation.walkthrough: First sense: the present participle of 'even', to make level. Second: the time of day when it grows dark.
explanation.definitionFit: Levelling a surface is smoothing it out; the hours after sunset are when night begins to fall.

clue.text: Trust worker with child

parts.note: to trust that something will happen is to expect it
a worker is a type of ant

explanation.surface: An employee entrusted with looking after a youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With child' looks like part of the worker's job but it is the definition: pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman with child is pregnant, awaiting a baby.

clue.text: Policemen blocking main road caught tart

indicators.note: the policemen sit inside the main road, blocking it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the A1 is Britain's main road north, written AI
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, plain-clothes police
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Detectives set up a roadblock on a main road and nab a woman of loose morals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tart' looks like a person in the police story, but here it is the adjective meaning sour. The A1 is Britain's longest numbered road.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe a sharp, sour taste, as of lemon or vinegar.

clue.text: My pleasure curtailed in an island

parts.note: 'Cor!' is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'My!'

indicators.note: curtailed means docked of its tail, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: fun is pleasure

explanation.surface: Someone's enjoyment is cut short while holidaying on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My pleasure' looks like a polite reply, but 'My' is the exclamation COR. 'In' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Corfu is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea.

clue.text: Choke, swallowing water with a hint of salt — it'll make you sick

indicators.note: swallowing means taking the other letters inside

parts.note: an engine that chokes stalls or dies
the sea is a body of water

indicators.note: only the first letter of salt is given

explanation.surface: Gagging on seawater with a salty taste is bound to make you ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Choke' looks like the illness's symptom, but it means stall, as an engine does; 'swallowing' puts the water and the first letter of salt inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Illness or sickness is caused by a disease.

clue.text: Stick with domestic 19th on course?

parts.note: a club is a heavy stick
house as an adjective means of the home, domestic

explanation.surface: A golf club and a home: where you end up after the eighteenth.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'nineteenth hole' is golfers' slang for the bar in the clubhouse after an eighteen-hole round.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers jokingly call the bar at the club, visited after the eighteen holes, the nineteenth hole.

clue.text: Retreating volunteers invite assault

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the volunteers' letters are read in reverse

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force
to invite trouble is to tempt it

explanation.surface: Volunteer soldiers fall back, which only encourages the enemy to attack.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA (Territorial Army) is the UK's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: An attempt on someone's life or on a summit is an attack or assault upon it.

clue.text: Clean and tidy dart found in western bar

indicators.note: the dart is found inside the bar, so one piece sits within the other
in an across clue, going west means reading right to left, so the bar's letters run backwards

parts.note: a pub is a bar
to dart is to rush

explanation.surface: A dart is discovered lodged in a saloon in the Wild West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Western bar' suggests a cowboy saloon, but 'western' signals reading the word for bar backwards, giving BUP, with RUSH placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To brush up a room is to give it a quick cleaning and smartening.

clue.text: We work and sleep, me and you, for the most part knackered

indicators.note: knackered is British slang for broken or exhausted, so the letters are rearranged
most of the word, all but its last letter, is used

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Workers complain that they and their partner are mostly too exhausted to do anything but sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the most part' trims YOU to YO; 'knackered' then scrambles SLEEP, ME and YO.
explanation.definitionFit: Staff on a payroll might describe themselves as the ones who do the work.

clue.text: Calm Conservative shifting unknown chap leading universal party

indicators.note: the chap goes in front of universal, leading it
the Conservative letter is shifted to another spot within the word for calm

parts.note: placid means calm
Y is an unknown quantity in algebra
MR is the title of a chap, a man
U is the film certificate for universal viewing

explanation.surface: A calm Tory changes sides, with some unnamed man heading a party for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shifting' moves the C of PLACID to the end, giving PLAIDC. Plaid Cymru is the Welsh nationalist political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaid Cymru is a Welsh political party, its name Welsh for 'Party of Wales'.

clue.text: Commander is horrified, losing way

indicators.note: losing means the word for way is taken away from the longer word

parts.note: to be aghast is to be horrified
ST, short for street, is a way

explanation.surface: An officer is appalled at going astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is horrified' gives AGHAST (is aghast), with 'losing' removing ST.
explanation.definitionFit: An agha was a military commander or chief officer in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Follow master's doctrine

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
an MA is a Master of Arts degree

explanation.surface: A disciple adopts their teacher's beliefs.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogma is a set of principles laid down as undeniably true, a creed.

clue.text: Fruit packed without one box-that's different!

indicators.note: the fruit is packed around the outside, so the other pieces go within

parts.note: a date is a fruit
I is the Roman numeral one
to spar is to box

explanation.surface: Fruit is packed without a single box, which is unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a container for the fruit, but it is the verb, to spar.
explanation.definitionFit: Disparate things are fundamentally unlike, dissimilar.

clue.text: Licked pulp of apple pud

indicators.note: making a pulp of something mashes it, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly finished off the mashed remains of an apple pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulp of' mashes APPLE PUD into a new order. Pud is British informal for pudding or dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: To lap up food is to take it up with the tongue, as a cat does milk.

clue.text: Plastic lay regularly in the open, melting

indicators.note: the regular letters go inside the rearranged ones
melting changes the shape of the words the open, so their letters are rearranged
take every other letter of lay, starting with the first

explanation.surface: Plastic laid out in the open air is melting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' gives L and Y from LAY; 'melting' rearranges THE OPEN into POTHENE, with LY going in.
explanation.definitionFit: Polythene is a common lightweight plastic used for bags and sheeting.

clue.text: Penning a little, I attempt correspondence

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, so the little bit is held inside the other letters

parts.note: a try is an attempt
some is a little, an amount

explanation.surface: A writer, dashing off a few lines, tries their hand at letter-writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' and 'correspondence' paint a letter-writer, but 'correspondence' is the mathematical sense: a one-to-one mapping preserving distance.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry it is a mapping that keeps distances equal, so shapes correspond exactly.

clue.text: Where you'll find the most expensive accommodation on board?

definitions.text: Where you'll find the most expensive accommodation on board?

parts.words: Where you'll find the most expensive accommodation on board?
parts.note: the board is a game board, not a ship: the priciest property square on the London edition of the property-trading game

explanation.surface: Asking which cabins on a cruise ship cost the most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a ship, but it is the Monopoly board: in the UK edition the dearest property is a smart London district.
explanation.definitionFit: In UK Monopoly, the costliest square is this exclusive London district.

clue.text: Relax on toilet, sitting effortlessly at the start

parts.note: loo is British slang for toilet

indicators.note: take the opening letter of each of the two words before this phrase

explanation.surface: Unwind on the lavatory, sitting there with no effort at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is a link word placing the pieces side by side. Loose here is the verb, to slacken or release.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose a grip or a knot is to slacken it, to let it go.

clue.text: Postponed revolution that's partly over?

parts.note: a postponed event is off
a spin is a turning, a revolution

explanation.surface: A delayed turn that is partly finished.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six balls; off spin is a style of bowling that may make up part of one.
explanation.definitionFit: Off spin is a cricket bowling style, so it can form part of an over of six balls.

clue.text: Blue follower of royal?

explanation.surface: A sailor in dark blue serving the Crown.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Navy is Britain's fleet, so this word follows 'royal'; navy is also a dark blue.
explanation.definitionFit: Navy is a dark shade of blue; it is also the word that comes after 'Royal' in Britain's naval service.

clue.text: Square from which knight starts today

explanation.surface: A chessboard square where a knight begins its move this very day.
explanation.walkthrough: The number is a perfect square (five times five). The chess picture misleads: the second half refers to the day's date, since the number names the day of the month the puzzle ran.
explanation.definitionFit: Five times five gives this number, so it is a square; it also names a calendar date.

clue.text: Mark two

explanation.surface: Making a pair of marks.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Twain was the American author; twain is also an old word for two.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Clemens; 'twain' is archaic for a pair.

clue.text: Back-slang is viewed, to some extent, as something rude

indicators.note: back means the letters are read in reverse
only part of the words is used, a run of letters hidden inside them

explanation.surface: Back-slang is seen, to some degree, as rather vulgar.
explanation.walkthrough: Back-slang is real word play spelling words backwards, which makes 'Back' sit unnoticed. In Britain a two-fingered V-sign, palm inward, is an insulting gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the two-fingered gesture with the palm inward is an obscene insult.

clue.text: Conductor finds Indian prince in a state

indicators.note: the prince sits within the state's abbreviation

parts.note: KAN is an abbreviation of Kansas, a US state
a raja is an Indian prince

explanation.surface: A maestro discovers a maharaja living in one of the American states.
explanation.walkthrough: Herbert von Karajan was the Austrian conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert von Karajan was a famous orchestral conductor.

clue.text: Misery caused by ultimately sad song about a strange feeling

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word sad

parts.note: ESP, extrasensory perception, is an uncanny feeling or sixth sense
the song is about, on the subject of, the strange feeling, so it follows that piece

explanation.surface: Gloom brought on by a mournful tune about an eerie sensation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' here means on the subject of: the song is about the feeling, so that piece comes first, with 'caused by' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Despair is utter hopelessness, a deep wretchedness.

clue.text: Wandering speaker ranted to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An orator rambling off the point launched into a tirade.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts at the end of 'speaker' and finishes inside 'ranted'.
explanation.definitionFit: Errant means roving or straying, as in a knight errant who travels in search of adventure.

clue.text: Flag news, stopping labourer

indicators.note: the news acts as a stopper placed inside the labourer

parts.note: a peon is an unskilled labourer in Latin America
N is short for new, so news is two of them, NN

explanation.surface: A headline report interrupts a worker's day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' could be a verb meaning tire; here it is a noun, a long narrow streamer on a lance.
explanation.definitionFit: A pennon is a long tapering pennant or streamer flown from a lance or mast.
